items.stem: A program moves words in the same sentence closer together. King and queen share several sentences, and king and hospital never appear together. What will the map show at the end?

options.text: King and queen end up close together, and king and hospital end up far apart.
options.feedback: Words that share sentences are pulled together. Words that never share a sentence are only pushed apart.

options.text: All the words end up in the same place after enough sentences.
options.feedback: Every sentence pulls its own words together, and all words also push each other apart a little. The map spreads into groups.

options.text: King and hospital end up close together, because both are common words.
options.feedback: Closeness depends on appearing in the same sentences. How common a word is has no effect.

options.text: The words stay where they started, because positions are never updated.
options.feedback: Each sentence moves the words in it. After many sentences the positions are very different.

items.stem: A colleague says someone must have labeled the royalty words in advance, or they could not form a cluster. What does the demo show?

options.text: The only input was fourteen sentences, so the clusters come from words appearing together.
options.feedback: The colors on the map are added afterward to show the groups. The training never uses them.

options.text: The program contains a dictionary of word meanings that says which words are about royalty.
options.feedback: There is no dictionary. The program moves words according to which sentences they appear in.

options.text: The groups form only because someone chose the starting positions by hand to favor them.
options.feedback: The starting positions are random. The groups come from the sentences.

options.text: The clusters form because the words were typed into the program in alphabetical order.
options.feedback: The order of the words in the list has no effect on where they end up.

items.stem: The small demo produces clear clusters, but it cannot reproduce arithmetic such as king minus man plus woman. Why?

options.text: It needs each word in thousands of contexts, which fourteen sentences cannot supply.
options.feedback: Real training uses billions of words. A small corpus is enough for clusters and too small for the finer patterns.

options.text: The demo has only two dimensions, and the arithmetic needs exactly three of them.
options.feedback: Real models use hundreds of dimensions. The main limit here is the amount and variety of text.

options.text: The demo never pushes words apart, so the groups never separate properly.
options.feedback: All words push apart a little in every step. That is how the groups separate.

options.text: Word arithmetic works only for the names of places and the names of people.
options.feedback: The arithmetic works for many kinds of relationships when there is enough text.
